title: Kubernetes on-prem handoff blueprint: Metal + vSphere bootstrap
content:
Purpose:
This is a working blueprint for operational handoff and runbook-style steps to bootstrap Kubernetes clusters in customer on-prem environments that use either bare metal provisioning (BMC/IPMI or Tinkerbell-style pipelines) or vSphere-managed VM pools. Target audience: SREs, Solutions Engineers, and field engineers who will do the initial boots, run the Terraform modules, and execute controlled upgrades.

Scope and assumptions:
- Scope: initial cluster bootstrap, Terraform module notes for infra, and a safe rolling upgrade plan. Not covering application-level CI.
- Assumes customer has provided: network ranges, gateway, DNS entries, vault/KMS access for secrets, BMC credentials (for baremetal) or vSphere credentials and datacenter/cluster folder info (for vSphere).
- Assumes private registry access (or image pull-through cache) is configured if air-gapped.
- Minimum infra: 3 control plane nodes, 3 worker nodes for production; test clusters may be 1 control-plane + 2 workers.

Inventory checklist (pre-checks before any provisioning):
- Confirm IP allocation plan and DHCP scope or static lease plan.
- Confirm BMC reachability (IPMI/Redfish), test credentials.
- Confirm vSphere API access and folder/cluster permissions.
- Verify NTP sources and time skew < 2s across hosts.
- Validate HSM/KMS access for encryption keys (if using customer-managed keys).
- Certificate authority choice: customer-provided or self-signed via Bootstrap CA?
- Confirm load balancer plan (NSX/MetalLB/HAProxy) and IP(s) reserved.
- Confirm storage backend: CSI options available (Ceph, NetApp, vSAN, local-path).
- Confirm SSH bastion host and jumpbox details.

High-level workflow (two paths: baremetal vs vSphere):
1) Common prep: validate DNS + IPs, set up Terraform remote state backend (S3-compatible or cloud storage with locking), create secrets in Vault, record all artifact versions.
2a) Baremetal path: use provisioning pipeline to PXE boot nodes into installer image (we use a metalctl-curtin flow here). After nodes come up, call infra Terraform to create nodepool representations and inject kubeadm join tokens.
2b) vSphere path: create VM templates, clone control-plane and worker VMs via terraform-provider-vsphere, ensure guest tools and cloud-init scripts are attached for first-boot provisioning.
3) Bootstrap control plane: use kubeadm init with kubeadm config referencing certificate SANs and external etcd if applicable. Use the control-plane machine bootstrap to apply RBAC and core add-ons (coredns, kube-proxy).
4) Join workers: run kubeadm join with --cri-socket and confirm node readiness.
5) Apply post-bootstrap components: CNI, CSI drivers, ingress controller, monitoring (Prometheus), logging (FluentBit).

Terraform modules and patterns (notes and recommendations):
- Module breakdown we recommend: network/, dns/, lb/, controlplane/, nodepool/, provisioning/ (BMC or vsphere), storage/. Keep modules small and composable.
- State: remote backend S3-compatible (minio) with Dynamo-style lock (consul or built-in locking) for on-prem.
- Secrets: do not store secrets in tfstate. Use Vault integration (vault provider or external secret injection).
- Idempotency: module outputs should include machine IDs, IPs, and provisioning status flags to enable reconciliation on re-run.
- Example variables to expose at top-level: cluster_name, k8s_version, pod_cidr, service_cidr, control_plane_count, worker_pools (list), vsphere_datacenter, bmc_gateway.
- Outputs to create: kubeconfig_path, lb_ips, control_plane_nodes, nodepool_ids, storage_class_names.
- Versioning: pin provider versions strictly and include module version tags in the repo.
- Backward-compatible changes: when modifying a module that affects resource names, provide a migration plan and mapping table to avoid resource recreation.

Sample Terraform usage snippet (conceptual):
- root main.tf calls: module.network, module.dns, module.lb, module.provisioning, module.controlplane, module.nodepool
- run: terraform init -backend-config=prod-backend.hcl
- plan: terraform plan -var-file=site-prod.tfvars
- apply: terraform apply -auto-approve -var-file=site-prod.tfvars

Provisioning specifics (baremetal):
- Use a provisioning module that: registers BMCs, configures ipxe templates, uploads curtin images for first-boot, and annotates inventory with MAC -> IP mappings.
- Keep a manual override list for stubborn servers (manual IP + user-data injection).
- Ensure isolation of provisioning network: once nodes are provisioned and healthy on the production network, revoke provisioning network access.

Provisioning specifics (vSphere):
- Use provider 'vsphere' with templates baked for required OS and container runtime (containerd).
- cloud-init user-data to run kubeadm join and fetch secrets from Vault via a short-lived token.
- Ensure vSphere customization spec sets network adapter order and hostname template.

Bootstrap/configuration sequencing and timing expectations:
- Expected time: 30–90 minutes for control plane provisioning and initial kubeadm init on a reasonably provisioned environment (network and storage pre-validated).
- Longer for air-gapped, as images and packages must be mirrored.

Upgrade plan (safe rolling upgrade blueprint):
Principles: minimize control-plane disruption, keep API available, respect control-plane quorum, verify backups, and ensure non-destructive automation.
Pre-upgrade checks:
- Run cluster health check script (krew + kc plugin or custom): nodes Ready, no CrashLoopBackOffs, no Pending volumes, all DaemonSets updated.
- Backup etcd snapshot to an external location (encrypted), test restore plan in staging.
- Tag current manifests and Terraform ref in version control.
- Notify stakeholders and set maintenance window.

Control plane upgrade steps (kubeadm flavor):
1) Upgrade kubeadm on first control plane node (sudo apt-get install kubeadm=version).
2) kubeadm upgrade plan
3) kubeadm upgrade apply vX.Y.Z (on leader) -> this upgrades control-plane static pods on that node. Wait for API to be healthy.
4) Repeat for remaining control plane nodes one-at-a-time, verifying etcd health after each node.

Worker node upgrade steps:
- Cordon node: kubectl cordon <node>
- Drain node gracefully (kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data)
- Upgrade kubelet and kube-proxy packages and restart kubelet
- Reboot if kernel updates applied
- Uncordon node and verify pod readiness
- If using scale sets (or vSphere templates), consider replacing node via nodepool lifecycle to ensure fresh image with new runtime version.

Add-on upgrade notes:
- CNI: ensure the CNI plugin supports target k8s version. Upgrade CNI early in a staging cluster and verify network policies.
- CSI: kubectl apply new driver manifests against CSI operator pattern, ensure volumes remain Bound and no detach failures.
- Ingress/LoadBalancer: test failover of LB and verify session affinity settings.

Rollback plan:
- If control plane becomes non-functional: restore etcd snapshot to a new control plane (staging) and compare. Keep the ability to spin up a temporary control-plane VM set (or use offline control plane images).
- For worker regressions: drain and roll back to previous image/template or revert terraform change and run apply.

Smoke tests and validation after upgrade:
- kube-apiserver accessible and responds to /healthz
- run sample e2e smoke tests (DNS resolution, CRUD on a simple Deployment, PV/PVC lifecycle)
- validate Prometheus alerting rules and no new critical alerts for 30m
- synthetic latency checks for common API operations

Operational gotchas and troubleshooting tips:
- DNS flaps during bootstrap usually come from duplicate CIDR or wrong CoreDNS config; check CoreDNS logs and node resolv.conf.
- Image pull failures: verify image-mirror and registry auth; check containerd config and systemd-reload.
- Flaky BMC: sometimes IPMI resets are required; temporarily escalate to physical hands-on for BMC firmware flakiness.

Runbook snippets (quick commands):
- drain: kubectl drain NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
- uncordon: kubectl uncordon NODE
- check etcd health: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 endpoint health --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/client.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/client.key
- snapshot etcd: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /tmp/etcd-snap.db --endpoints=... --cacert=...

Post-handoff tasks for field engineer:
- Populate Confluence Handoff page with final IPs, inventory, Terraform state backend location, and kubeconfig TTL policy.
- Create runbook for daily health checks (automated via cronjob or alerting).

Open questions / TODO (for team closure before marking final):
- Decide policy for kubelet kernel upgrades (reboot cadence) per customer SLA.
- Finalize exact repo layout for terraform modules (single monorepo vs multi-repo).
- Document air-gapped image mirroring steps and size estimate for images per k8s version.

References and inspiration:
- internal: Confluence Onprem Handoff Checklist (link in metadata), existing terraform modules repo
- upstream: kubeadm upgrade docs, kubelet and kube-proxy compatibility matrix

Notes: this document is intentionally pragmatic and terse. It's a working blueprint intended to be iterated after the first two on-site deployments. Add additional site-specific sections as needed (power constraints, switch VLAN configs, BMC quirks).
